[00:00:03] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we can do intros quick; I'm Jordan, AE on the account at Redwood. Maya's our SE, she'll cover the technical bits.
[00:00:12] Rajiv Menon: Hi, Rajiv here, CTO at Tempest. We run most infra on AWS, currently proxying some calls to a mix of vendor APIs and an in-house open model. We're exploring moving to something more predictable-cost and lower-latency.
[00:00:28] Maya Chen: hi! quick note, sorry my audio is a bit crunchy. can you give a sense of primary workloads? generation, chat, embeddings?
[00:00:35] Claire Dupree: primarily chatified generation for customer support agents + some doc summarization and retrieval-augmented generation. embeddings for search, but main pain is long context, about 20-40k tokens for multi-doc cases.
[00:00:52] Sam Ortiz: and we need tool-calling — DB writes and a knowledge-retriever that calls a vector DB plus some internal APIs. Latency target is sub-250ms p95 for short queries, for long-context flows we're OK with 500-800ms but cost matters.
[00:01:10] Jordan Patel: got it. So main requirements: long context (~32k), tool-calling support, multilingual support (you mentioned French and Japanese?), and compliance/VPC. Is that right?
[00:01:19] Rajiv Menon: exactly. our users are global. performance in EN/FR/JP needs parity-ish. Also curious about fine-tuning vs instruction-tuning with open models.
[00:01:30] Maya Chen: great. on the model side we usually evaluate a few open families — Llama-derived, Mistral, and newer opt variants — and pick quantization and compilation strategies based on context length. Redwood can serve model variants in hosted mode, or give dedicated pools if you want isolation and predictable throughput. For private, we do VPC/private control plane with KMS integration.
[00:01:52] Claire Dupree: how much work is it to get tool-calling in hosted? we need outbound callbacks to our API and some custom function schema.
[00:02:02] Jordan Patel: hosted supports function/tool calling and structured outputs; callbacks are supported but for sensitive data we recommend dedicated or private so the customer has network controls. we do outbound webhooks from the runtime; there are retry/backoff semantics.
[00:02:20] Lena Fischer: on the security side, SOC 2 plus ISO would be required, and we need audit logs, SSO via SAML, SCIM provisioning, and BYOK/KMS. Also data residency for EU customers.
[00:02:34] Maya Chen: we can provide SOC2 and ISO docs, audit logs are in Redwood Console, and enterprise private deployments can be pinned to regions or on-prem. KMS/HSM integrations exist for private installs.
[00:02:48] Rajiv Menon: sweet. about model selection — do you benchmark for multilingual quality out of the box or we need to provide evaluation prompts?
[00:02:56] Maya Chen: we typically ask for a seed prompt set so we can run the evals. Redwood Optimize also has quality monitoring and will flag regressions. For context length, there's an engineering tradeoff — model architecture + kernel selection; beyond 32k we often recommend segmented KV caching with continuous attention where supported, or using a retrieval-first strategy to reduce active context size.
[00:03:20] Claire Dupree: what's the real difference between Dedicated and Private for us?:
[00:03:25] Jordan Patel: Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity inside Redwood's network — predictable throughput and isolation from noisy neighbors, but still managed by Redwood control plane. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you customer-managed networking and optionally an on-prem package where you control the control plane and keys. Dedicated is faster to onboard; Private takes more time but satisfies strict compliance.
[00:03:47] Sam Ortiz: cost-wise, how does dedicated compare to hosted? we have heavy throughput during business hours.
[00:03:53] Maya Chen: hosted is usage-based — good for spiky or initially light workloads. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity which reduces per-token cost at scale; there's a base monthly commit. We can model your QPS and token patterns and show break-even.
[00:04:08] Rajiv Menon: for long context — do you run custom kernels or use vendor runtimes? we need to know about memory pressure on 80GB A100 equivalents.
[00:04:16] Maya Chen: Redwood's runtime picks optimized kernels based on architecture and sequence length distribution. For 32k+, we leverage continuous KV cache paths, attention optimizations, and sometimes different quantization (q4/q8) depending on quality targets. We'll include kernel/throughput numbers in the benchmark.
[00:04:34] Claire Dupree: any support for offloading or sharded kv-cache for extremely long docs?
[00:04:39] Maya Chen: yes, we have techniques — sharded KV between GPUs and prefix caching — but implementation depends on the model family. some open families have better support. we'll surface candidate models that support efficient long-context.
[00:04:51] Jordan Patel: any existing vendors you're comparing?
[00:04:54] Rajiv Menon: we're talking to OpenAI for hosted, Anthropic for chat primitives, and evaluating Mistral self-hosted. Cost is a big driver.
[00:05:03] Jordan Patel: noted. we can include a competitor comparison and rough cost model.
[00:05:08] Claire Dupree: do you support function calling schemas — like typed outputs and validation? we need strict schema enforcement for some flows.
[00:05:15] Maya Chen: yes, structured outputs and validation hooks are supported; we can show examples. For high-assurance flows we recommend turning on guarded decoding and schema enforcement at the runtime layer.
[00:05:28] Sam Ortiz: about telemetry — can we get token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency?
[00:05:33] Jordan Patel: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and traces. We'll make sure the demo tenant has the same.
[00:05:42] Lena Fischer: data retention — do you log raw prompts? we need options to obfuscate or not store PII.
[00:05:49] Maya Chen: by default we log request/response for observability, but in Dedicated/Private customers can choose different retention policies or disable storage. We also support redaction and token-level metadata.
[00:06:03] Rajiv Menon: timeline — we plan to pick a partner in 6-8 weeks and run a 2-4 week pilot. Is that workable?
[00:06:10] Jordan Patel: absolutely. typical flow: pilot (benchmarks + evals), then dedicated commit or private onboarding. we'll scope the pilot in the next call.
[00:06:18] Claire Dupree: on benchmarks, we need to evaluate in EN/FR/JP. we also want hallucination/regression monitoring.
[00:06:25] Maya Chen: Redwood Optimize supports quality monitoring and eval hooks; we'll set up evals across locales and provide regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
[00:06:34] Rajiv Menon: anything we should share to make benchmarking faster?
[00:06:38] Maya Chen: sample prompt set, expected per-session token sizes, peak QPS, and example multi-step tool flows. If you can share a small representative dataset (anonymized), we'll use that in the pilot.
[00:06:50] Rajiv Menon: we'll prepare that.
[00:06:54] Jordan Patel: quick recap — Jordan to send pricing and comparison, Maya to draft benchmark plan, Tempest to share prompts and telemetry targets, Lena to compile compliance questions. We aim to reconvene for a technical deep dive week of August 9. Any other blockers?
[00:07:12] Lena Fischer: nothing else from security — just confirm KMS options and whether keys can be customer-managed in dedicated.
[00:07:19] Maya Chen: yes, KMS support exists for private and customer-managed keys for dedicated can be arranged — we'll include details.
[00:07:27] Sam Ortiz: thanks, this was helpful.
[00:07:29] Jordan Patel: thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and calendar invite.
